common_misconceptions: believes wrapping the two statements in a transaction is by itself sufficient
adds a lock without considering the throughput cost on a hot row

expected_concepts.hint: a read-modify-write cycle where the second write overwrites the first
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE holds a row lock so the second reader waits
version column in the WHERE clause; zero rows updated means retry
UPDATE ... SET n = n + 10 removes the read-modify-write entirely

follow_up_seeds: Which approach would you choose for a single very hot counter row?
reference_answer: This is a lost update: both transactions read the same value, compute from it, and the later write silently overwrites the earlier one. A transaction alone does not prevent it at READ COMMITTED - both reads are legal and both writes are legal. Pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the row before reading it, which takes an exclusive row lock so the second transaction blocks until the first commits and then reads the updated value. It is simple and always correct, and it costs throughput - requests serialise on that row, and holding the lock across any slow work in the transaction turns it into a queue, with deadlock risk if lock order is inconsistent. Optimistic: keep a version column, read it with the row, and write UPDATE ... SET value = ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If another transaction won, zero rows are affected and the application retries. No locks are held, so it scales well under low contention, and the costs are wasted work plus mandatory retry logic that must be present everywhere the row is written. Under high contention on one row, the retries make it worse than a lock. Best of all here, if the operation really is just an increment, write UPDATE ... SET n = n + 10, which the database performs atomically and which removes the read-modify-write cycle altogether.
text: Two requests read the same row, each adds 10 to the value they read, and each writes the result back. The row ends up 10 higher rather than 20. Name this problem, and describe two different ways to prevent it - one pessimistic and one optimistic - including the cost of each.

common_misconceptions: expects the database to hang rather than abort one of the transactions
treats a deadlock error as a database bug rather than a condition to retry

expected_concepts.hint: each holds a lock the other needs, producing a cycle in the wait-for graph
the database finds the cycle and aborts one transaction as the victim
always acquire rows in a consistent global order, which makes a cycle impossible
shorter transactions holding fewer locks reduce the window in which a cycle can form

follow_up_seeds: How would you find the two statements involved after the fact?
reference_answer: A deadlock needs a cycle in the wait-for graph: transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and asks for row 2, while B holds row 2 and asks for row 1. Neither can proceed and neither will release, so waiting forever is the only alternative to intervention. The classic example is two code paths that update the same pair of rows in opposite orders, which is easy to create accidentally when the order comes from an unsorted collection or from user input. Databases run a periodic deadlock detector, find the cycle, and abort one transaction as the victim with a specific error - in PostgreSQL SQLSTATE 40P01 - releasing its locks so the other proceeds. The victim's work is rolled back entirely. The most effective prevention is consistent lock ordering: always acquire rows in the same deterministic order, for example ascending primary key, so no cycle can form. Sorting the ids before the loop that updates them is often a one-line fix for a recurring production deadlock. Supporting measures: keep transactions short and never hold locks across a network call or user think-time; take the most contended lock first; and treat the deadlock error as retryable, since even with good discipline lock upgrades and index-level locks can still produce one.
text: Explain the conditions under which two transactions deadlock in a relational database, what the database does when it detects one, and the single most effective application-side change that prevents most deadlocks in practice.

common_misconceptions: concludes the planner is broken and reaches for a hint or a forced index
assumes any query mentioning an indexed column is able to use the index

expected_concepts.hint: a predicate matching a large fraction of rows makes a scan cheaper
wrapping the column in a function or casting it hides the indexed value
stale statistics produce a row estimate that justifies the wrong plan
compare estimated with actual rows, and test the hypothesis by changing one thing

follow_up_seeds: What is the risk of using enable_seqscan = off to test a hypothesis?
reference_answer: First, low selectivity: if the predicate matches a large fraction of the table - roughly more than five to ten percent - an index scan means many random single-page reads plus heap lookups, which costs more than reading the table sequentially, so the planner is right. Confirm by running the predicate as a COUNT and comparing it with the table's row count, and by checking whether the estimated row count in EXPLAIN is large. Second, a non-sargable predicate: WHERE lower(email) = ... , WHERE created_at::date = ... , or a comparison whose types force an implicit cast, all ask for a value the index does not store. Confirm by rewriting the predicate to compare the bare column, for example a half-open timestamp range instead of a cast to date, and re-running EXPLAIN; the fix is that rewrite or an expression index. Third, stale or missing statistics: the planner's estimate is far from reality, so it costs the wrong plan. Confirm by comparing the estimated and actual row counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE - a large discrepancy is the signal - then run ANALYZE and retry. Other legitimate reasons worth mentioning are a very small table, where a scan is simply cheaper, and a partial index whose WHERE clause does not cover the query. Forcing the index without establishing the cause treats the symptom.
text: A query filters on a column that has an index, but EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. Give three distinct reasons a planner can legitimately ignore an available index, and for each say how you would confirm it is the reason in this case.

common_misconceptions: believes READ COMMITTED can return uncommitted data
assumes REPEATABLE READ prevents all write anomalies, including write skew

expected_concepts.hint: each statement sees a fresh snapshot of committed data
the whole transaction sees one snapshot taken at its first read
the same row read twice in one transaction returns different values
match the level to whether the transaction reasons across multiple reads

follow_up_seeds: What is a phantom read, and which level is the first to prevent it?
reference_answer: Interleaving: transaction A reads row X and gets 100. Transaction B updates X to 150 and commits. A reads X again. Under READ COMMITTED, every statement takes a new snapshot of committed data, so A's second read returns 150 - a non-repeatable read, and A has now computed with two different values of the same row. Under REPEATABLE READ, A's snapshot is fixed at its first read, so the second read still returns 100 and A sees a single consistent point in time. Neither level ever exposes uncommitted data; that is READ UNCOMMITTED, which PostgreSQL does not implement separately. The practical default for a web application is READ COMMITTED - it is PostgreSQL's default, it holds no read snapshot across statements so it produces less bloat and fewer conflicts, and typical request handlers do one logical operation. Escalate deliberately: a transaction that reads several rows and reasons across them, such as a report or a balance check followed by a write, wants REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE. The important caveat is that REPEATABLE READ can abort with a serialization failure, so any code using it must be safe to retry - and it still permits write skew, which only SERIALIZABLE prevents.
text: Compare READ COMMITTED with REPEATABLE READ. Give a concrete two-transaction interleaving that behaves differently under the two levels, name the anomaly involved, and say which level you would default to for a web application and why.

common_misconceptions: believes ON and WHERE are interchangeable for outer joins
expects NULL = 'x' to evaluate to false rather than UNKNOWN

expected_concepts.hint: LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows, padding the right columns with NULL
a comparison against NULL is UNKNOWN, so the padded rows fail the filter
conditions on the right table belong in ON; conditions on the left in WHERE
missing rows in a report are the usual symptom

follow_up_seeds: How would you list customers who have never placed an order?
reference_answer: An INNER JOIN emits only pairs of rows that satisfy the join condition. A LEFT JOIN emits those, plus every left row that matched nothing, with the right table's columns filled with NULL. The order of evaluation is what causes the trap: the join runs first and produces the NULL-padded rows, then the WHERE clause filters that result. A predicate such as WHERE o.status = 'paid' is UNKNOWN for a NULL-padded row - in three-valued logic a comparison with NULL is neither true nor false - and WHERE keeps only rows where the predicate is true, so exactly the rows the LEFT JOIN was written to preserve are discarded, silently reproducing an inner join. The fix is to move the condition into the ON clause: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' restricts which right rows are eligible to match while still keeping unmatched left rows. The rule of thumb is that a filter on the outer-joined table belongs in ON, and a filter on the preserved table belongs in WHERE. The deliberate exception is WHERE o.id IS NULL, which is the idiom for finding left rows with no match at all.
text: Explain the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN. Then explain why putting a condition on the right-hand table in the WHERE clause of a LEFT JOIN usually turns it back into an inner join, and where that condition belongs instead.

common_misconceptions: denormalises before establishing that the join is actually the bottleneck
maintains the copy with application code in a separate transaction from the write

expected_concepts.hint: read cost falls, write cost and correctness risk rise
the copy can disagree with its source, and nothing in the schema prevents it
let the database own the derivation and the refresh
decide explicitly how out of date the report may be

follow_up_seeds: How would you detect that the denormalised copy has drifted?
reference_answer: The gain is a read that touches one table instead of five, removing join and planner work from the hot path. What you give up is single-source-of-truth: the copy is derived data, and derived data drifts. Nothing in the schema prevents the copy from disagreeing with the tables it came from, so correctness moves from a database constraint into human discipline, which is the real cost. Mechanisms, roughly in order of safety: a materialised view, where the database owns the definition and the refresh, so the derivation cannot be forgotten and REFRESH CONCURRENTLY keeps reads available; triggers, which update the copy in the same transaction as the write, correct but adding write latency and lock footprint; an asynchronous job or CDC consumer, which decouples the write path at the price of a bounded staleness window; and application-level dual writes, which are the most common and the most error-prone, because every future write path must remember. Before any of this, confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the join is the bottleneck rather than a missing index or a bad cardinality estimate, and decide the tolerable staleness explicitly - a report that may be five minutes old is a much cheaper system than one that may not.
text: A reporting endpoint joins five normalised tables and has become too slow. The team proposes storing a denormalised copy of the joined result. Explain what you gain, which guarantee you give up, and the mechanisms available for keeping the denormalised copy correct.

common_misconceptions: attributes the guarantee to consistency or durability rather than to atomicity
assumes two separate statements are atomic without an explicit transaction

expected_concepts.hint: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, each a distinct promise
all statements in the transaction take effect or none do
an uncommitted transaction is rolled back when the database restarts
both statements must be inside one transaction for the guarantee to apply

follow_up_seeds: What if the credit goes to a different service, not a second table?
reference_answer: Atomicity: a transaction's statements all take effect or none do; there is no partial outcome. Consistency: a committed transaction moves the database from one state satisfying its declared constraints to another - it is about constraints such as foreign keys and CHECKs, not about application correctness in general. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not observe each other's intermediate states, to a degree set by the isolation level. Durability: once commit returns, the effects survive a crash. The half-transfer is prevented by atomicity. With both the debit and the credit inside one transaction, a crash before commit leaves the transaction uncommitted, and recovery rolls it back using the write-ahead log, so neither statement is visible. Durability is a different promise - that a transfer which did commit is not lost - and consistency would only catch the half-transfer if a constraint happened to encode the invariant, which for a balance total it usually cannot. The practical caveat worth stating is that the guarantee depends on both statements actually being in one transaction: two auto-committed statements from the application are two transactions, and no ACID property spans them.
text: State what each letter of ACID guarantees. Then take a transfer of money between two accounts and explain precisely which of those guarantees prevents the money from being deducted from one account but never credited to the other when the process crashes midway.

common_misconceptions: believes commit flushes the modified table pages to disk
treats a successful write() call as durable without an fsync

expected_concepts.hint: the change is logged and flushed before commit returns; pages are written later
commit means the log record is on stable storage, not that the table is updated
an OS write only reaches the page cache; fsync is what forces the device
asynchronous commit trades a bounded window of committed-but-lost transactions for throughput

follow_up_seeds: When is asynchronous commit an acceptable setting for real workloads?
reference_answer: Durability comes from write-ahead logging. Before any modified page may be written back, a log record describing the change is appended to the WAL, and at commit that log is flushed to stable storage with an fsync; only then does commit return. The table's own pages stay dirty in the buffer pool and are written later by a checkpointer. Writing the data pages at commit would be far slower - they are scattered across the file, so it is random I/O, whereas the WAL is a single sequential append that a disk handles at full speed. It would also be unsafe on its own, since a crash midway through writing a set of pages leaves a torn state with nothing recording the intent. On restart, recovery replays committed log records whose pages had not been flushed and rolls back uncommitted ones. The fsync matters because an ordinary write only reaches the operating system's page cache, which power loss discards. Disabling synchronous commit lets commit return once the record is in the WAL buffer, before the flush: throughput improves markedly, and the price is a bounded window - typically a fraction of a second - in which acknowledged transactions can be lost after a crash. Note that atomicity is unaffected; the database does not become corrupt, it just loses recent commits.
text: A database reports a transaction as committed. Explain the mechanism that makes that promise survive an immediate power loss, why writing the modified data pages themselves is not what provides it, and what an operator gives up by turning synchronous commit off.

common_misconceptions: believes overflow is impossible because both indices are valid array positions
mixes a half-open interval with an inclusive loop condition and loops forever

expected_concepts.hint: the target, if present, always lies within the current search interval
the interval must shrink on every iteration or the loop hangs
lo + hi can exceed the integer range; use lo + (hi - lo) / 2
the condition must match whether the interval is closed or half-open

follow_up_seeds: How would you adapt it to find the first element greater than a target?
reference_answer: State the invariant first and the rest follows: if the target is in the array, it is in the current interval. With a closed interval [lo, hi] the loop must run while lo <= hi, because a one-element interval lo == hi still needs to be examined, and the branches must move past the midpoint - lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1 - so the interval strictly shrinks and the loop terminates. With a half-open interval [lo, hi) the condition is lo < hi and the update is hi = mid, which is correct only because mid < hi always holds under floor division. Mixing the two conventions is the classic infinite loop: hi = mid with lo <= hi never terminates when lo == hi. On the midpoint, lo + hi can exceed the maximum signed integer even though lo and hi are both valid indices - the famous bug in java.util.Arrays.binarySearch, live for nine years. Writing lo + (hi - lo) / 2 computes the same value without an intermediate that can overflow. Python's arbitrary-precision ints make this specific bug impossible, which is worth saying rather than pretending the concern is universal.
text: Binary search is famously easy to get wrong. Describe the loop invariant your implementation maintains, explain how you decide between lo <= hi and lo < hi as the loop condition, and say why computing the midpoint as (lo + hi) / 2 is a latent bug in a fixed-width integer language.

common_misconceptions: claims adding a constant to every edge weight fixes the problem
conflates negative edges with negative cycles and calls the problem undefined

expected_concepts.hint: a settled node's distance is final, which assumes paths cannot get cheaper later
a later negative edge can undercut a distance already committed to
a concrete graph with numbers, not a verbal assertion
relaxes all edges V-1 times and can detect negative cycles

follow_up_seeds: When would you use Johnson's algorithm instead?
reference_answer: Take S -> A with weight 2, S -> B with weight 5, and B -> A with weight -4. Dijkstra settles S, then extracts A at 2 and treats that distance as final. It later extracts B at 5 and relaxes B -> A, computing 5 + (-4) = 1 - but A is already settled, so the improvement is discarded and the algorithm reports 2 when the true shortest distance to A is 1. Note that the negative edge has to arrive after the node it improves has been settled; an example where the improvement is found while the node is still tentative will silently give the right answer and prove nothing. The property that breaks is the greedy invariant: Dijkstra assumes that once a node is extracted with the minimum tentative distance, no future relaxation can improve it, which holds only when all edge weights are non-negative, so every path extension is non-decreasing. A negative edge makes a longer path cheaper later, invalidating the finality of settled nodes. Adding a constant to all weights does not fix it, because it penalises paths in proportion to their edge count and so changes which path is shortest. Bellman-Ford is the correct algorithm: it relaxes every edge V - 1 times in O(V * E), makes no greedy commitment, and a further relaxation pass that still improves a distance proves a negative cycle exists - at which point 'shortest path' genuinely is undefined.
text: Dijkstra's algorithm is often summarised as 'shortest path, but with weights'. Using a small concrete example, show how it can return a wrong answer when one edge has a negative weight, explain which property of the algorithm the negative edge breaks, and name an algorithm that handles negative edges correctly.

common_misconceptions: justifies the greedy by trying examples rather than by an exchange argument
assumes sorting by start time or by shortest duration is equally valid

expected_concepts.hint: some optimal solution contains the earliest-finishing interval
swap the first interval of any optimal solution for the greedy one without loss
sort by end time, take an interval whenever it starts after the last one taken
weighted intervals break it; that variant needs dynamic programming

follow_up_seeds: Sketch the DP recurrence for the weighted version.
reference_answer: The proof is an exchange argument. Let g be the interval with the earliest end time and let O be any optimal solution, with o its first interval by end time. Since g ends no later than o, replacing o with g in O leaves every remaining interval in O still compatible - they all start after o ends, hence after g ends - so O' = O minus o plus g is also optimal and has the same size. Some optimal solution therefore contains the greedy choice, and applying the argument inductively to the remaining subproblem shows the greedy solution is optimal overall. This is what distinguishes a proof from examples: it quantifies over all optimal solutions rather than testing a few inputs. Choosing earliest end time is what leaves the maximum room for the rest, which is why sorting by start time or by shortest duration both fail - a single early-starting interval that runs all day, or a short interval overlapping two disjoint ones, defeats them. The greedy also fails as soon as intervals carry weights and the objective becomes maximum total weight: one high-value long interval can beat many cheap short ones, there is no exchange argument, and the correct solution is a dynamic program over intervals sorted by end time using a predecessor lookup.
text: Given n intervals with start and end times, repeatedly choosing the interval with the earliest end time yields a maximum-size set of non-overlapping intervals. Explain why this greedy choice is provably optimal rather than merely plausible, and describe a scheduling variant in which the same greedy strategy stops being optimal.

common_misconceptions: argues O(1) point lookup beats O(log n) regardless of the query being asked
suggests iterating the whole hash map and filtering, treating O(n) per query as acceptable

expected_concepts.hint: hashing destroys order, so neighbouring keys are not neighbouring in memory
the workload is a range scan, not a point lookup
a balanced BST, skip list, B-tree or sorted array supports range scans
choose by the dominant access pattern, not by the fastest headline complexity

follow_up_seeds: When would you keep both structures over the same data?
reference_answer: A hash map answers 'what is the value for exactly this key' in O(1), and nothing else. The workload described is a range scan, and a hash function deliberately destroys the ordering of keys, so there is no way to enumerate the keys between two bounds without inspecting every entry - turning each query into O(n). The correct choice is an ordered structure: a balanced binary search tree, a skip list, a B-tree, or simply a sorted array if the data is append-only in time order. All of them find the lower bound in O(log n) and then walk forward in O(k) for k matching results, which is proportional to the size of the answer rather than the size of the data. In a database this is the same argument as choosing a B-tree index over a hash index. The general principle worth stating is that a data structure is chosen by the dominant access pattern, and that O(1) for the wrong operation is worse than O(log n) for the right one.
text: A service stores millions of events keyed by timestamp, and its most frequent query is 'give me every event between 09:00 and 09:05'. A teammate proposes a hash map from timestamp to event because lookups are O(1). Explain why a hash map is the wrong structure for this access pattern, and what you would use instead.

common_misconceptions: asserts the pointers meet at the start of the cycle rather than somewhere inside it
claims the fast pointer could jump over the slow one and miss it entirely

expected_concepts.hint: slow moves one step, fast moves two; they meet inside the cycle or fast hits null
inside the cycle the gap closes by one per step, so it must reach zero
restart one pointer at the head and advance both by one to find the entry node
O(1) versus O(n) for a visited set

follow_up_seeds: How would you also report the length of the cycle?
reference_answer: Advance a slow pointer one node per step and a fast pointer two. If the list terminates, fast reaches null and there is no cycle. If there is a cycle, both pointers eventually enter it, and thereafter the fast pointer gains exactly one position per step on the slow one. A gap that decreases by exactly one per step cannot be skipped over, so it must hit zero: they meet. That is the correctness argument, and it is the part most answers omit. To find the entry node, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the first node of the cycle, which follows from the meeting point being congruent to the cycle entry modulo the cycle length. The algorithm uses O(1) extra space and O(n) time. The hash-set alternative - walk the list recording visited nodes and stop at the first repeat - is simpler and also O(n) time, but O(n) space, and it is the better choice when clarity matters more than memory. A strong answer names that tradeoff rather than treating Floyd's algorithm as automatically superior.
text: Describe Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm for a singly linked list: how the two pointers move, why they are guaranteed to meet if a cycle exists, and how you would then locate the first node of the cycle. State its space complexity and contrast that with the hash-set approach.

common_misconceptions: counts openers and closers and concludes equal counts means balanced
forgets that leftover openers at the end of the string are a failure

expected_concepts.hint: push openers, pop and compare on each closer
correct nesting means the most recent unmatched opener must close first
O(n) time, one pass over the string
a closer with an empty stack fails; a non-empty stack at the end also fails

follow_up_seeds: How would you extend this to report the index where it first went wrong?
reference_answer: Scan the string once. Push every opening bracket onto a stack. On every closing bracket, fail immediately if the stack is empty, otherwise pop and fail if the popped opener is not the matching type. After the scan, the string is balanced only if the stack is empty. A stack is the right structure because correct nesting is exactly a last-in-first-out constraint: the bracket that must close next is always the most recently opened unmatched one. Both failure checks matter and are the usual omission - a closing bracket with nothing to match, and unmatched openers left at the end. The algorithm is O(n) time and O(n) space in the worst case, when every character is an opening bracket. A counting approach is not equivalent: ([)] has equal counts of each type and is still incorrectly nested, which is the cleanest way to show why the order, not the tally, is what is being checked.
text: Given a string containing only the characters (, ), [, ], { and }, describe an algorithm that decides whether the brackets are correctly balanced and nested. Say which data structure you would use and why that structure in particular, and give the time and space complexity.

common_misconceptions: transfers all elements on every dequeue, making the structure genuinely O(n) per operation
claims worst-case O(1) dequeue because most dequeues are cheap

expected_concepts.hint: FIFO built from two LIFO structures by reversing once
an inbox stack for pushes, an outbox stack that is only refilled when empty
each element is moved between stacks at most once, so n operations cost O(n)
a single dequeue can be O(n); the amortised bound is the correct claim

follow_up_seeds: Where would this structure be a bad choice despite the amortised bound?
reference_answer: Keep an inbox stack and an outbox stack. Enqueue always pushes onto the inbox, which is O(1). Dequeue pops the outbox; if the outbox is empty, first pop every element from the inbox and push it onto the outbox, which reverses the order and puts the oldest element on top, then pop. The critical detail is that the transfer happens only when the outbox is empty - transferring on every dequeue destroys the bound. Each element is pushed to the inbox once, moved to the outbox at most once, and popped once, so any sequence of n operations does O(n) total work and dequeue is O(1) amortised. It is not O(1) worst case: the dequeue that triggers a transfer of k elements costs O(k). Stating the amortised bound and explicitly disclaiming the worst-case one is the answer being looked for; this is also a good example of why such a structure is unsuitable for a hard real-time deadline, where the worst case is the only number that matters.
text: Implement a FIFO queue using only two LIFO stacks, supporting enqueue and dequeue. Describe the algorithm, then analyse the cost of a sequence of n operations. Is dequeue O(1) in the worst case, O(1) amortised, or neither?

common_misconceptions: assumes the compiler always rewrites the loop into a builder
believes the cost is the allocation count rather than the repeated copying

expected_concepts.hint: each concatenation allocates a new string and copies both operands
the growing prefix is recopied every iteration, giving 1 + 2 + ... + n copies
O(n * m) copies overall, quadratic in total output length
collect the pieces in a list and join once, or use a StringBuilder

follow_up_seeds: Does the same reasoning apply to list concatenation in a loop?
reference_answer: Because strings are immutable, s + chunk cannot extend s in place: the runtime allocates a fresh string of the combined length and copies both operands into it. The accumulated prefix therefore gets copied again on every iteration, so the total work is proportional to 1 + 2 + ... + n, that is O(n^2) in the number of chunks or, stated in characters, quadratic in the length of the final string. The fix is to stop building intermediate results: append the chunks to a list and call ''.join(parts) once in Python, or use StringBuilder in Java, both of which write into a geometrically growing buffer and produce the final string in a single pass, giving O(total length). A strong answer notes that CPython has an in-place optimisation for the special case of a string with a single reference, which is exactly why the bug survives small benchmarks and reappears in production; it is an implementation detail, not a guarantee to design around.
text: In a language with immutable strings, such as Python or Java, building a result by repeatedly writing s = s + chunk inside a loop over n chunks is far slower than it looks. Explain what the runtime actually does on each iteration, give the total time complexity of the loop, and describe the idiomatic fix.

common_misconceptions: proposes raising the timeouts along the path instead of decoupling the work
spawns a background thread in the web process and treats the job as safely queued

expected_concepts.hint: enqueue the job, let a worker pool run it outside the request
a two-minute request ties up a connection and dies to any timeout in the path
return a job id and expose a status endpoint, or notify by webhook or push
the user gets an immediate acknowledgement and a visible progress state

follow_up_seeds: What guarantees that the job is not lost between the upload and the queue?
reference_answer: A two-minute request fails for structural reasons, not because it is slow. Every timeout in the path - browser, load balancer, proxy, gateway - is shorter than that, so the connection is cut and the client cannot tell whether the work succeeded. It occupies a worker or connection slot for two minutes, so a modest number of concurrent uploads exhausts the pool and takes down unrelated endpoints. A deploy or crash mid-request loses the work with no record that it was ever requested, and the client's only recovery is to retry the whole upload. It also couples two very different scaling profiles: the API is I/O-bound and the transcoder is CPU-bound, and they cannot be scaled independently while they share a process. Instead, the request should store the uploaded file, write a job record, enqueue it, and return 202 Accepted with a job id and a status URL. A separate worker pool consumes the queue. The client learns of completion by polling the status endpoint, which is simplest and adequate for a two-minute job; by a webhook if the caller is another service; or by a server-sent event or push notification for a live UI. Details worth stating: the status should distinguish queued, running, succeeded and failed, and carry the error on failure; the enqueue must be reliable, so writing the job row and enqueueing should be in one transaction or use an outbox, otherwise a crash between them loses the job silently; and a background thread in the web process is not a queue, because it dies with the process.
text: Uploading a video triggers transcoding that takes about two minutes. Explain why this work should not happen inside the HTTP request that uploaded the file, what the API should return instead, and how the client learns that the work has finished.

common_misconceptions: asks for exactly-once delivery from the broker instead of idempotent processing
deduplicates in an in-memory set, which does not survive a restart or a second consumer

expected_concepts.hint: a message may be redelivered after a crash or a missed acknowledgement
processing the same message twice must have the same effect as once
a stable business key stored with a uniqueness constraint, checked in the same transaction
park a repeatedly failing message so it stops blocking or looping, and can be inspected

follow_up_seeds: How would you safely replay a batch of dead-lettered messages?
reference_answer: At-least-once means the broker will redeliver whenever it cannot confirm a message was handled - the consumer crashed after charging but before acknowledging, the acknowledgement was lost, or a visibility timeout expired while the work was still running. Combined with a side effect as irreversible as a card charge, redelivery means charging the customer twice, and no amount of broker configuration removes the possibility, because the failure is in the gap between doing the work and recording that it was done. The consumer must therefore be idempotent: processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once. Implement it with a stable idempotency key derived from the business event rather than from the delivery - an order id, not a message id, since a retry may carry a fresh message id - stored in a table with a unique constraint, and written in the same transaction as the effect. The consumer inserts the key and does the work atomically, and a duplicate key collision means the work is already done, so acknowledge and stop. When the effect is in an external system, use that system's own idempotency key, which every payment provider offers for this exact reason. A dead-letter queue handles the other failure: a message that fails every time - malformed payload, a deleted referenced record, a bug - would otherwise be retried forever, consuming capacity and, on an ordered queue, blocking everything behind it. After a bounded number of attempts, ideally with backoff, the message is moved to the DLQ where it stops harming throughput and can be inspected, fixed and replayed. A non-empty DLQ should alert; a DLQ nobody watches is just a slower way to drop messages.
text: A message queue guarantees at-least-once delivery, and your consumer charges a customer's card. Explain the hazard this specific combination creates, what property the consumer must therefore guarantee and how you would implement it, and the purpose of a dead-letter queue when one message keeps failing.

common_misconceptions: proposes a longer TTL, which reduces the frequency of the stampede but not its size
believes adding database capacity is a fix rather than a way to survive it

expected_concepts.hint: expiry synchronises every reader into a simultaneous miss on the same key
concurrent misses each independently do the expensive recomputation
one request recomputes under a lock; the others wait for or reuse its result
refresh slightly early with a random chance, so misses do not align

follow_up_seeds: What happens under coalescing if the recomputation itself fails?
reference_answer: This is a cache stampede, sometimes called dog-piling, and the concurrent recomputation is a thundering herd. It is caused by the expiry design because a TTL makes the entry vanish at one instant for every reader simultaneously; from that instant until the first recomputation completes, every arriving request misses, and each one independently starts the same expensive query. The severity is set by arrival rate multiplied by recomputation time, so a slower query makes it dramatically worse, and a longer TTL makes it rarer but no smaller. It is worst precisely for the hottest keys, which is why it tends to arrive as an outage rather than as degradation. Mitigation one, request coalescing: the first miss takes a lock on the key and recomputes while the others either wait for its result or briefly serve the stale value. This collapses N recomputations into one; the costs are a lock to manage, a decision about what waiters do if the recomputation is slow or fails, and the risk that the lock itself becomes a bottleneck. Mitigation two, probabilistic early expiry: as an entry approaches its TTL, each reader has a small and increasing chance of refreshing it early, so refreshes are spread across time and one unlucky reader pays while everyone else gets a hit. It needs no coordination, and it costs some redundant refreshes and slightly more complex read logic. Related approaches are serving stale content while refreshing in the background, and adding jitter to TTLs so keys written together do not expire together - which is the same class of bug at the level of the whole cache rather than one key.
text: A popular cache entry with a 60-second TTL expires at peak traffic, and the database immediately receives thousands of identical queries. Name this failure, explain why it is a property of the expiry design rather than of the traffic level, and describe two mitigations and what each one costs.

common_misconceptions: chooses strong consistency everywhere as the safe default without pricing it
reads 'eventual' as 'a second or two' rather than as an unbounded promise of convergence

expected_concepts.hint: every read sees the latest committed write, at the price of coordination
replicas converge if writes stop; no bound on when unless one is stated
derive the requirement from what a stale read would actually cause
consensus adds latency on every write and reduces availability under partition

follow_up_seeds: Which session guarantees would you add to the like counter, and why?
reference_answer: The balance needs strong consistency, because the decision made from the read has external consequences that cannot be undone: a stale balance permits an overdraft or a double spend, and reconciling that afterwards is a business problem, not a technical one. The like counter tolerates eventual consistency, because a count that is briefly a few behind causes no incorrect decision and no user notices. Eventual consistency promises only convergence: if writes stop, all replicas will agree eventually. It gives no bound on how long, and no guarantee about what a reader sees in the meantime - a read can go backwards, and two users can see different values at the same moment. In practice systems layer stronger session guarantees on top, such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads, because those are what users actually notice. Demanding strong consistency for both costs latency and availability. Every write must be coordinated - a quorum or a consensus round, so a cross-region write carries at least one round trip and often more - and during a network partition the minority side must refuse writes rather than serve them, so availability falls exactly when you need it. It also concentrates writes, which makes the like counter, the highest-volume and least important write in the product, the thing that limits throughput. The point worth making is that consistency is chosen per operation, not per system: the same product can and should run a consensus-backed store for money and an eventually consistent, conflict-free counter for likes.
text: One product contains both an account balance and a 'number of likes' counter. Explain which of these needs strong consistency and which tolerates eventual consistency, what 'eventual' actually promises, and what it would cost to demand strong consistency for both.

common_misconceptions: believes retries are always safe because the request eventually succeeds
sets one global timeout without regard to the caller's own deadline

expected_concepts.hint: a call with no deadline holds a connection and a worker indefinitely
retries multiply load onto a dependency that is already struggling
spread retries in time and randomise them so clients do not synchronise
A's thread or connection pool exhausts, so A fails requests unrelated to B

follow_up_seeds: How would you choose the timeout value for a dependency you do not own?
reference_answer: Without a timeout, each call to B occupies one of A's workers or connections until B eventually answers. As B slows, in-flight calls accumulate: arrival rate multiplied by response time is the concurrency required, so a tenfold slowdown needs tenfold the pool. When the pool is exhausted, A can serve nothing at all - including requests that never touch B - so B's degradation becomes A's total outage. That is a cascading failure, and the missing timeout is what propagates it. Naive retries make it worse in a specific way: retrying a slow call multiplies the load arriving at B at exactly the moment it is least able to cope, so the system applies maximum pressure to its weakest point. Worse, retries compose - three layers each retrying three times is twenty-seven calls for one request - and when many clients retry on the same schedule they synchronise into waves. What to configure: an explicit connect and read timeout on every outbound call, set from the p99 of the healthy dependency rather than from a round number; a deadline propagated from the inbound request, so a caller that has already spent its budget does not start work nobody is waiting for; a small bounded number of retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and only for idempotent operations; a retry budget capping retries as a fraction of total traffic, so retries can never dominate; a bulkhead - a separate connection pool per dependency - so B cannot consume all of A's capacity; and a circuit breaker to stop calling B when failure is the expected outcome. Failing fast is the goal: a quick error preserves capacity, whereas an unbounded wait spends it.
text: Service A calls service B. B slows down badly but does not return errors. Explain how a missing timeout in A turns B's slowness into A's outage, why a naive retry policy makes the situation worse rather than better, and what you would configure instead.

common_misconceptions: adds a high-cardinality label such as user id to a metric to answer per-user questions
believes traces make logs unnecessary

expected_concepts.hint: events with detail, aggregates over time, and one request across services
match the signal to whether the question is about one request or about a population
metrics are cheap because they aggregate; a per-user label destroys that
a trace, found by request id, shows where the time went

follow_up_seeds: What sampling strategy keeps traces useful for rare slow requests?
reference_answer: Metrics are numeric aggregates over time. They answer 'is the error rate rising', 'what is p99 latency this week', 'are we near capacity' - and they answer badly anything about one specific request, because aggregation has discarded the individual. They are cheap precisely because of that aggregation, which is why adding a user id or a request id as a label is a mistake: cardinality explodes and the backend's cost with it. Logs are discrete events with arbitrary detail. They answer 'what exactly happened in this request', 'what was the payload that caused this exception' - and they answer badly 'what is the trend across a billion requests', since computing that from raw logs is slow and expensive. Traces follow one request across service boundaries as a tree of timed spans. They answer 'where did the time go' and 'which of the eleven services this request touched was the slow one' - and they answer badly questions about aggregate health, particularly when sampling means most requests were never traced. For one user reporting one slow request, start with the trace, provided you can find it: get a request or trace id from the report or from an access log filtered by user and time, then open that trace and read the span breakdown, which usually localises the problem in seconds. Then use logs from that trace id for the detail the spans do not carry, and metrics to decide whether this was one user's problem or the visible edge of a wider one. The practical requirement underneath all of this is correlation: a trace id propagated through every service and attached to every log line, so the three signals are three views of the same event rather than three separate systems.
text: Logs, metrics and distributed traces overlap but answer different questions. For each of the three, give one question it answers well and one it answers badly, and say which you would reach for first when a single user reports that one particular request was slow.

common_misconceptions: treats horizontal scaling as strictly superior in all situations
ignores that a vertical resize usually requires a restart

expected_concepts.hint: a bigger machine versus more machines
the largest available instance, and a superlinear price curve before it
distribution buys capacity by adding coordination, partial failure and consistency questions
one machine is one point of failure, however large it is

follow_up_seeds: What would make you scale out before you had to?
reference_answer: Vertical scaling means giving the same instance more CPU, memory or faster storage. It is simple - no code changes, no coordination, and the program keeps its single-process assumptions - and it is often the cheapest fix for a real problem in engineer-hours. Horizontal scaling means running more instances behind a balancer, which is what gives near-unbounded capacity and, importantly, redundancy. Vertical is genuinely better for a stateful single-writer system: a primary relational database is the standard example, because sharding it introduces cross-shard joins, distributed transactions and a rebalancing problem, whereas doubling its memory so the working set fits in cache may buy a year of headroom for a day of work. The same argument applies to a workload that is hard to parallelise, such as a single large in-memory computation. The limits that force horizontal are: the largest instance available is a hard ceiling; price rises superlinearly well before that ceiling; resizing usually needs a restart, so scaling itself causes downtime; and one machine is one failure domain, so no amount of vertical scaling gives availability. That last point is the important one - horizontal scaling is often adopted for redundancy rather than for throughput, and a system that must survive the loss of a machine has to be horizontal regardless of its load. In practice the sequence is to scale up first, and out when capacity, cost or availability demands it.
text: Compare scaling a service vertically with scaling it horizontally. Give one workload where vertical scaling is genuinely the better engineering decision, and name the limit that eventually forces a horizontal approach.

common_misconceptions: stores image bytes in a database column for transactional convenience
chooses a document store for profiles purely because a profile is a nested object

expected_concepts.hint: read/write ratio, query shape, size per item, retention and durability needs
how the data is queried decides the store, not how it looks
large immutable blobs belong in object storage with a URL in the database
immutable, time-ordered, queried by range and retained cheaply

follow_up_seeds: How do you keep the object store and the database from drifting apart?
reference_answer: Profiles: a relational table. The access pattern is point lookup by user id, occasional queries by an indexed attribute, and updates that must be consistent with the rest of the account - which wants transactions, constraints and joins to other user data. A document store is defensible if profiles are genuinely schemaless and always fetched whole, but 'it is a nested object' is the wrong reason on its own, and PostgreSQL's JSONB covers that case without giving up the relational parts. Audit trail: append-only, never updated, written far more often than read, read by time range and by subject, and retained for a long time. That points to a table partitioned by time - so old partitions can be dropped or archived instantly - or to a purpose-built log or time-series store if the volume justifies one. The key properties are cheap sequential appends, range scans, and inexpensive retention, plus the integrity requirement that it be genuinely immutable, enforced by permissions. Images: object storage such as S3, with only the key and metadata in the database. They are large, immutable, served directly to browsers and often through a CDN, and never queried by content. Putting the bytes in a database column inflates every backup, pollutes the buffer cache with data no query filters on, and routes every download through the application; the tradeoff is that the object store and the database can now disagree, so orphaned objects need a cleanup process. The general principle worth stating is that the access pattern - query shape, mutability, item size, read/write ratio, retention - determines the store, and the same data reshaped for a different pattern may legitimately live in two places.
text: A service stores user profiles, an append-only audit trail, and uploaded profile images. Recommend a storage technology for each, and justify every choice by the access pattern rather than by the shape of the data.
